title: Binomial cumulative tail probability for manufacturing defect batch
scenario_markdown: An electronics manufacturing line produces batches of $n = 12$ high-precision sensors. The defect probability for each sensor is $p = 0.15$, and sensor failures occur independently. Quality assurance protocol triggers a full calibration audit if a batch contains at least $3$ defective sensors ($X \ge 3$). Determine the probability $P(X \ge 3)$ that a randomly inspected batch triggers an audit.
assumptions: Fixed sample size of n = 12 independent sensor trials
Constant defect probability p = 0.15 per sensor
Each sensor is classified as defective or conforming (binary outcome)
source_refs: Course Module 2: Discrete Random Variables & Probability Distributions

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: n = 12, p = 0.15. P(X=0) = 0.14224, P(X=1) = 0.30122, P(X=2) = 0.29236. Cumulative P(X<=2) = 0.73582. Upper tail P(X>=3) = 1 - 0.73582 = 0.26418 (26.42%). Excel: =1 - BINOM.DIST(2, 12, 0.15, TRUE). Distractor tests off-by-one boundary error 1 - P(X<=3).

stages.prompt_markdown: Which complement relationship correctly sets up the cumulative tail probability $P(X \ge 3)$?

options.hint_markdown: Because $X = 3$ satisfies the condition 'at least 3', it must not be subtracted away. Subtract only outcomes less than 3 ($X \le 2$).
'At least 3' includes $3, 4, 5, \dots, 12$; its complement is $0, 1,$ and $2$, not just the point $X = 3$.

stages.explanation_markdown: In discrete distributions, boundary points matter critically. The event $X \ge 3$ comprises outcomes $\{3, 4, 5, \dots, 12\}$. The complementary outcomes are $\{0, 1, 2\}$, which corresponds to the cumulative probability $P(X \le 2)$. Therefore, $P(X \ge 3) = 1 - P(X \le 2)$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the cumulative probability of finding at most $2$ defective sensors: $P(X \le 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2)$.

options.hint_markdown: Cumulative probability $P(X \le 2)$ requires adding $P(0) + P(1) + P(2)$, not just $P(2)$.
Probabilities must be computed using the Binomial PMF $\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$, not linear scaling.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the audit trigger probability $P(X \ge 3) = 1 - P(X \le 2)$ and identify the matching Excel formula.

options.hint_markdown: Entering 3 into BINOM.DIST subtracts $P(X = 3)$, which erroneously computes $P(X \ge 4)$.
$0.1720$ is the probability of exactly $3$ defects ($P(X = 3)$), not at least $3$ defects ($P(X \ge 3)$).

stages.explanation_markdown: Subtracting the lower cumulative probability from $1$ yields $P(X \ge 3) = 1 - 0.73582 = 0.26418$, or approximately $0.2642$ ($26.42\%$). There is roughly a $26.4\%$ probability that an audit will be triggered. In Excel: `=1 - BINOM.DIST(2, 12, 0.15, TRUE)`.
